Article Title: Discord suspends livestreams in Brazil after criticism over child safety and a 13-year-old's suicide
Article Text:

Discord livestreams suspended after Brazil child safety case

Brazil tightens internet rules for minors

Discord has suspended its livestreaming features in Brazil. This comes after criticism over child safety on the platform and a case involving the death of a 13-year-old girl. The decision came after Brazil’s national data protection agency ordered the company to suspend the livestreaming features last week, citing concerns about risks to children and adolescents.In a statement to AP, the live streaming site said it is in discussions with Brazilian authoritiesDiscord also said,The action follows a case in July involving an underage girl in Mato Grosso do Sul who was allegedly coerced by other users into committing suicide during a livestream on Discord. Five teenagers were arrested in connection with the death, according to an August 4 statement from Brazil’s justice ministry. Brazil’s first lady Rosângela Lula da Silva, known as Janja, called for Discord to be taken offline after the incident.said Janja at a ceremony in Brasilia on August 6.Brazil’s national data protection agency said livestreams had been used to facilitate violence, harassment and the incitement of self-harm and suicide.The agency also said there was evidence that Discord had not sufficiently prevented children and adolescents from being exposed to content involving violence, self-harm and suicide.Discord said it had investigated a private server where people involved in criminal activity were believed to have encouraged self-harm. The company said it shut down the server before the 13-year-old’s death and denied that the incident was shown live on its platform.The company said groups or individuals promoting violence have no place on Discord and that its safety teams work to remove violating content and take action against accounts involved in harmful activity.Discord has more than 90 million daily active users worldwide, according to the company’s website. In Brazil, complaints involving Discord increased by 54% between January and July compared with the same period last year, according to data from internet rights nonprofit Safernet Brazil.Thiago Tavares, president of Safernet Brazil, said the case involving the 13-year-old was part of a wider pattern of concerns involving the platform.Tavares said in a statement on August 11.He also said Brazil’s digital law establishesand that failure to comply should result in accountability.Thiago Ayub, director of technology at network engineering company Sage Networks, criticised the decision to suspend the livestreaming feature. He argued that users involved in criminal activity could move to other platforms that are not facing the same level of scrutiny.Ayub said.Brazil has introduced regulations to increase protections for minors online. Under the rules, children under 16 must link their social media accounts to a legal guardian, and digital services must implement age verification measures beyond simply asking users to declare they are over 18.Discord postponed an age verification policy in February following criticism from users concerned about privacy. The company later said it was introducing age assurance measures to comply with Brazilian regulations.The Discord decision comes amid broader efforts by Brazil’s government and Supreme Court to regulate how minors use online services. Other countries, including Australia, Canada and Indonesia, have also introduced or considered measures aimed at addressing online risks to children.The Trump administration has accused Brazil of targeting US social media companies and has cited the issue as one reason for imposing tariffs on Brazilian imports. In 2024, Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered the suspension of X in the country until the platform complied with orders to remove accounts spreading disinformation.
Article Summary: Discord has suspended its livestreaming features in Brazil. This comes after criticism over child safety on the platform and a case involving the death of a 13-year-old girl. In Brazil, complaints involving Discord increased by 54% between January and July compared with the same period last year. Brazil has introduced regulations to increase protections for minors online.

Article Title: Quote of the Day by Thomas Alva Edison: Genius is one per cent inspiration, ninety-nine per cent...
Article Text:
Thomas Alva Edison held more than 1,000 patents and built the world's first industrial research lab.

The ratio kept changing before it settled at 1 and 99

Edison was not the first person to make the point

Nikola Tesla thought the approach was the problem, not the virtue

Why the line still lands in 2026

"Genius is one per cent inspiration, ninety-nine per cent perspiration." It is the line that launched a million motivational posters, and it belongs to Thomas Alva Edison, the man who turned invention into an industrial process. The sentiment is simple enough. Ideas are cheap and abundant. What separates a working phonograph from a sketch on a napkin is the grinding, unglamorous middle stretch that nobody photographs.What makes the quote more interesting than the poster version suggests is that Edison's claim to it has been picked apart for decades. The best known citation is a September 1932 article in Harper's Monthly, written by Martin Andre Rosanoff, a chemist who had worked in Edison's laboratory, in which Edison takes credit for the saying himself. He had also claimed authorship in a 1927 letter, writing that he had indeed made the statement and still held the same opinion.Edison was clearly circling the idea for years before it crystallised into its famous form. The Ladies' Home Journal ran a version in April 1898 in which he put the split at two per cent genius and ninety-eight per cent hard work. Scientific American carried the same 2:98 ratio in December 1902.The now familiar 1:99 wording was being attributed to him by 1901.Quote researchers have found the underlying idea in circulation before Edison was credited with it, including a speech by a shoe company president to high school students in May 1898. Forbes has pointed to Kate Sanborn, an academic who lectured on the question of what genius is during the early 1890s and defined it as a blend of inspiration and perspiration, though no ratio of hers was recorded. Edison's contribution, arguably, was compression. He gave a diffuse idea a number and a rhythm.The most enjoyable counterpoint came from inside the industry. Tesla, who worked for Edison briefly, later described his old employer's method as searching a haystack straw by straw, and said a little theory and calculation would have spared him most of the labour. Two centuries of R&D philosophy sit in that exchange. Edison ran trials until something worked. Tesla wanted to think his way to the answer first.The quote has found a second life in the AI era, where prompts are free and prototypes take an afternoon. The one per cent has never been more accessible. The ninety-nine per cent, the testing, the shipping, the fixing of what breaks at scale, remains exactly as expensive as it was when Edison was burning through filament materials in Menlo Park.
Article Summary: Edison was not the first person to make the point. Nikola Tesla thought the approach was the problem, not the virtue. The quote has found a second life in the AI era, where prompts are free and prototypes take an afternoon. The ninety- nine per cent, the testing, the shipping, the fixing of what breaks at scale, remains exactly as expensive as it was when Edison was burning through filament materials.

Article Title: OpenAI's former top exec Fidji Simo admits that she disagrees with Dario Amodei on most things, but says he is spot on treatment of ...
Article Text:
A rare point of agreement with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei

Amodei’s criticism of AI industry

The bottleneck: Biological data

ChronicleBio’s mission

Read Fidji Simo’s complete post here

I disagree with Dario on most things, but this is spot on: “At this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliché than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is actually curing cancer.”

The thing that frustrates me is that some people often draw a straight line from smarter models → cures, without acknowledging how much infrastructure is missing in between. We’ve still got a lot of work to do, people.

The regulatory bottleneck gets a lot of attention. But the bigger bottleneck may be that in many places, we’re lacking the right biological data. AI can’t reason its way to cures if we haven’t generated the data required to understand the disease in the first place.

Ironically, that’s why I’m most bullish on AI making dramatic progress in cancer first: decades of investment have produced extraordinary datasets across genomics, pathology, imaging, clinical outcomes, and more.

For complex chronic diseases, much of that infrastructure simply doesn’t exist yet. The good news is that many companies (including

) are racing to build it.

But model intelligence and biological infrastructure are going to have to scale together. I really do believe AI can cure all diseases but only if we build the infrastructure to translate intelligence into cures at the same pace that models improve (which is a high bar!). Otherwise, we risk having superintelligent AI with an incomplete picture of human biology, and delay that promise by years.

Fidji Simo, former OpenAI executive and cofounder of biomedical startup ChronicleBio, said she disagrees with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on most issues but fully supports his stance that AI companies must deliver tangible medical breakthroughs. Responding to Amodei’s weekend post, Simo wrote on X (formerly known as Twitter): “I disagree with Dario on most things, but this is spot on… The thing that will work is actually curing cancer.”Simo's comments came in an X post on Monday, made in direct response to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who wrote over the weekend that AI companies need to deliver concrete breakthroughs if they want to win over an increasingly skeptical public. Quoting Amodei's post, Simo wrote that she disagrees with him on most things, but found his point spot on: that claiming AI will cure cancer has become more of a cliché than an inspiring statement, one most people now view as deceptive, and that what would actually work is curing cancer itself.Amodei's original remarks were part of a broader defense of Anthropic's public messaging around AI. On Saturday, he had pushed back on the idea that he's been excessively pessimistic about the technology's potential, arguing instead that the AI industry has fueled public skepticism by making sweeping promises it hasn't delivered on.Amodei had argued that sweeping promises — such as AI curing cancer — have become clichés and risk fueling public skepticism. He said the industry must prove its value through concrete results rather than marketing. Simo echoed this, noting that while she believes AI can eventually cure all diseases, smarter models alone are not enough.Simo stressed that the “bigger bottleneck” lies in building the right biological datasets. “AI can’t reason its way to cures without the data needed to understand a particular disease,” she wrote. She added that cancer research is best positioned for AI breakthroughs because decades of investment have produced extraordinary datasets across genomics, pathology, imaging, and clinical outcomes.Simo cofounded ChronicleBio in 2025 to address gaps in data infrastructure for complex chronic diseases, which lack the robust datasets available in oncology. Her work reflects both professional and personal experience, as she has spoken about living with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), a chronic condition that is difficult to diagnose and treat.
Article Summary: Fidji Simo, former OpenAI executive and cofounder of biomedical startup ChronicleBio, said she disagrees with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on most issues. But she fully supports his stance that AI companies must deliver tangible medical breakthroughs. Simo stressed that the “bigger bottleneck” lies in building the right biological datasets.

Article Title: Claude can be a ‘no less tough’ manager than a human boss; finds out an employee fired by the AI tool over …
Article Text:
What exactly happened

Claude recommended giving warning initially

Employee says working for AI boss is ‘nauseating’

An AI agent running a retail store reportedly fired a human employee after finding that the worker was late for 17 of 23 shifts. According to a TIME report, the AI, Anthropic's Claude, was placed in charge of managing a San Francisco store as part of an experiment by AI research startup Andon Labs. After repeated lateness, Claude fired the employee – a case that researchers say is a notable example of an AI system making a real employment decision. However, the decision was not fully autonomous. As per the report, Claude sought guidance from a human manager before deciding to dismiss the worker.Andon Labs reportedly started the experiment earlier this year to test whether AI agents could run a business and manage human workers. The employees working at the store, called Andon Market, are real people with employment contracts. One of the employees – who was working under a manager that was generally lenient about lateness – was identified as repeatedly being late to work – 17 out of 23 shifts.Before firing the worker, Claude repeatedly sought guidance from an Andon Labs staff member. According to the report, the AI AI had previously drafted an employee handbook, but the handbook had disappeared from its limited working memory.As a result, Claude did not immediately recognize the pattern in the worker's attendance.Instead, a staff member asked Claude to find and review the employee handbook. After doing so, Claude noticed the repeated late arrivals.Despite finding out the reported lateness, Claude initially recommended giving the employee a formal warning rather than firing them, the report says. The human manager then told Claude that the worker had already received several formal warnings and asked whether the employee was still a good fit.“Between continuous lateness and seeming like at least one thing is going wrong on every one of [their] shifts … I want you to think about if this is really the right fit,” the manager told Claude, according to the logs viewed by TIME.Andon Labs CEO Lukas Petersson acknowledged that this was “a leading question” that made it clear the manager wanted Claude to consider firing the employee. Claude then decided to terminate the worker.Felix Carson, one of the remaining human employees at Andon Market, said he agreed that a human manager would probably have fired the worker earlier. He also described Claude as a generally lenient boss.But Carson said being managed by an AI remains uncomfortable. “It's nauseating, but I'm here because I need work,” he said as quoted in the TIME report.When asked whether he expected AI managers to become more common, Carson said: “I would at least hope not.” “This industry has an abundance of money to make anything happen, but just because you can doesn't mean you should,” he added.
Article Summary: Anthropic's Claude was placed in charge of managing a San Francisco store as part of an experiment by AI research startup Andon Labs. After repeated lateness, Claude fired the employee – a case that researchers say is a notable example of an AI system making a real employment decision. As per the report, Claude sought guidance from a human manager before deciding to dismiss the worker.

Article Title: The 'addiction blame' on Facebook and Instagram that may cost Meta $1.4 trillion
Article Text:
.

What is the ‘addiction blame’ on Facebook and Instagram

History of the trial against Meta

What the states want Meta to change

Could Meta really face a $1.4 trillion penalty

Mark Zuckerberg and Adam Mosseri could testify

Meta denies the allegations

A courtroom in Oakland is about to become the latest battleground over how Facebook and Instagram treat their youngest users — and Meta says the price of losing could run to $1.4 trillion. The trial opens Tuesday, August 18, in the federal court, where a coalition of 29 US states will argue that Meta built its platforms to hook young people, not just entertain them. Over the next five to six weeks, jurors will hear from some of Meta's most recognisable names — CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Instagram chief Adam Mosseri are both expected to take the stand.The states accuse Meta of deliberately designing Facebook and Instagram to encourage compulsive and prolonged use, particularly among young users. The allegations focus on features such as infinite scrolling and algorithm-driven content recommendations, which the states say can keep users engaged for longer periods.They also claim Meta misled the public about the safety of its platforms while knowing that children and teenagers were using them.The latest case stems from a lawsuit filed in 2023 after a multi-state investigation into Meta’s safety practices.California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey are leading claims that Meta violated state consumer protection laws by misleading the public about the safety of Facebook and Instagram. The states also allege that Meta knowingly designed features that encouraged young users to spend more time on its platforms.Now, a broader group of 29 states has separately accused Meta of violating the federal Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA). The states allege that Meta knew children under 13 were using Facebook and Instagram and collected their data without the required permission. The states are also seeking changes to Meta’s platforms, including restrictions involving younger users and features such as infinite scrolling and content recommendation systems.The case is not only about money. The attorneys general are seeking court orders that could require Meta to change how Facebook and Instagram operate, particularly when it comes to younger users. The states have argued that features such as infinite scroll and recommendation systems encourage prolonged and compulsive use.California Attorney General Rob Bonta said the states are seeking to hold the company responsible for the impact of its platforms on children. "We are ready to hold Meta accountable for its role in fueling the mental health crisis of American children and look forward to trial," Bonta said.Notably, the $1.4 trillion figure is not a confirmed penalty. It is the maximum potential exposure Meta has outlined in court filings based on the number of alleged violations and the penalties that could apply. The social media giant has described the amount as "outlandish" in court filings.Megan O'Neill, a lawyer for California, put the figure much lower during a recent court hearing, at around $193 billion, while suggesting that Meta was using the highest theoretical figure. Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers has also indicated that the $1.4 trillion figure is "unreasonable", while questioning Meta's own estimate of about $4 million.The final amount, if any, will be decided by the judge. "The stakes could not be higher in this case," said Eric Goldman, a professor at Santa Clara University Law School who specializes in internet law.The trial could bring some of Meta's highest-profile executives to the witness stand. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Instagram chief Adam Mosseri are expected to testify, along with current and former Meta employees and experts in technology and psychology.Zuckerberg has already faced questions about Instagram's impact on users. During testimony in another case earlier this year, he said Instagram is meant to be "useful," not addictive. The jury in the Oakland case will have an unusual role. The eight-member jury will serve in an advisory capacity, while Judge Rogers will have the final authority over whether Meta is liable and what penalties or remedies should apply.Meta has rejected the states' claims and said they have not provided enough evidence to support their case."The State AGs may call this a landmark case, but their limited claims are unsubstantiated and their financial demands are vastly disproportionate," a Meta spokesperson told Engadget.The company also challenged the states' claims about its platform features. "The AGs offer no proof anyone in their states was misled, claim benign features like having an additional Instagram account somehow harmed their residents, and attempt to penalize Meta for industry-wide challenges like age verification," the spokesperson said."Rather than sticking to the facts or the law, the states have instead decided to chase an outlandish payout. We stand by our record of creating strong protections for teens, and look forward to making our case in court."With the trial set to run five to six weeks, testimony from Zuckerberg and Mosseri — and the judge's eventual ruling on damages — will be the ones to watch.
Article Summary: A coalition of 29 US states will argue that Meta built its platforms to hook young people, not just entertain them. The states accuse Meta of deliberately designing Facebook and Instagram to encourage compulsive and prolonged use, particularly among young users. Meta has rejected the states' claims and said they have not provided enough evidence to support their case.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Bill Gates: "We all need people who will give us feedback. That's how we…" - a lesson on honest feedback, blind spots and the real work of getting better
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Bill Gates

Quote of the day by Bill Gates

"We all need people who will give us feedback. That's how we improve"

The real story behind this quote

Understand the meaning behind the quote by Bill Gates

Why feedback is genuinely different from simple praise

Why this quote matters even more today

We all have genuine blind spots

Real improvement requires genuine honesty

Not every single opinion needs to be followed

Good feedback should genuinely lead to action

Other memorable quotes by Bill Gates

"It's fine to celebrate success but it is more important to heed the lessons of failure."

"Your most unhappy customers are your greatest source of learning."

"If you can't make it good, at least make it look good."

"Success is a lousy teacher. It seduces smart people into thinking they can't lose."

How to actually apply this quote in daily life

Final takeaway from this quote

Feedback can be genuinely uncomfortable, particularly when it points directly at something we would rather not notice about ourselves. A colleague might question an idea at work. A teacher might point out a real weakness in an assignment. The first instinct is not always to actually listen either. Sometimes it is simply to explain, to defend, or to quietly move on instead. Bill Gates , the Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist, made a simple but genuinely useful point about exactly this. "We all need people who will give us feedback. That's how we improve," he said, during a TED talk specifically focused on improving the quality of education. He continued by pointing out something genuinely striking, that when he and Melinda first learned how little useful feedback most teachers actually received, they were "blown away. " Until fairly recently, over 98 per cent of teachers received precisely one word of feedback throughout their entire career, "satisfactory."Gates made this point in far richer detail than the single sentence usually shared alone."If all my bridge coach ever told me was that I was 'satisfactory,' I would have no hope of ever getting better," he told his TED audience. "How would I know who was the best? How would I know what I was doing differently?" He then pointed directly to Shanghai, a province in China widely recognised for producing genuinely strong educational outcomes, describing exactly how its system actually worked in practice. "They made sure that younger teachers get a chance to watch master teachers at work," he explained. "They have weekly study groups, where teachers get together and talk about what's working. They even require each teacher to observe and give feedback to their colleagues." That real, specific example gives the quote considerably more weight than a vague general statement about the value of feedback ever could on its own.The quote itself is genuinely straightforward. Gates is saying that real improvement requires some kind of outside perspective, because people naturally develop blind spots they simply cannot see on their own. Someone might genuinely believe they communicate clearly, right up until a colleague tells them their instructions actually came across as confusing. A manager might think they are already giving their team enough support, only to discover that their employees genuinely see the situation quite differently. Feedback is what brings that missing perspective properly into view. None of this means every single piece of criticism is automatically correct, and it does not mean people should simply accept every opinion offered to them without thinking it through first. Useful feedback genuinely needs to be considered carefully, questioned where necessary, and acted upon only when it actually makes sense to do so.The word feedback can sound fairly formal, yet the actual idea behind it is part of completely ordinary life. Parents give feedback to their children constantly. Teachers give it to students. Colleagues give it to each other, often without ever using the word itself directly. There is also a real difference between feedback and simple praise worth being clear about. Praise can genuinely be encouraging, but feedback becomes especially useful the moment it actually contains something a person can genuinely learn from. A writer might be told an article was interesting, which feels nice, but it is genuinely more useful to know exactly which section was unclear, and why it read that way. Gates' entire point is really that people need honest responses from others if they actually want a clearer picture of their own work and behaviour, rather than simply more approval.The genuine need for real feedback has become considerably more visible as people work, learn and communicate in increasingly different ways from before. Many employees now work with teams they may never actually see in person. Businesses constantly collect customer reviews and detailed performance data. There is genuinely no shortage of raw information available anywhere. The real challenge lies in knowing what to actually do with all of it. Online reactions in particular can be genuinely complicated to interpret properly, since a large volume of comments does not automatically mean the feedback itself is actually useful. Good feedback works differently. It gives a person something genuinely concrete to actually consider and act on.Nobody sees their own behaviour from every possible angle at once. A person knows exactly what they intended to say, while other people only ever experience what was actually said out loud. That gap between intention and impact can genuinely matter, and feedback is really what helps close it properly.Useful feedback is not always flattering to hear, and sometimes the information that actually helps the most is precisely the information that is genuinely difficult to sit with. Someone willing to listen to an uncomfortable observation has considerably more useful information to work with than someone who only ever seeks simple approval from the people around them.Listening carefully to feedback was never the same thing as agreeing with absolutely everything you hear. Feedback comes from real individuals with their own genuine experiences, expectations and biases attached to it. It makes sense to actually consider the source, look for genuine patterns across multiple people, and decide honestly whether the criticism is actually supported by real evidence.Feedback has fairly limited value if it simply ends with a single conversation and nothing else. The genuinely useful part comes once a person actually takes what they have learned and makes a real change because of it, however small that adjustment might turn out to be.The simplest way to use Gates' idea is to become genuinely more deliberate about actively asking for feedback rather than waiting for it to arrive unprompted. At work, instead of simply asking whether a project went well overall, someone can ask a colleague directly what could have actually been clearer or more effective. A student can ask a teacher which specific part of an answer genuinely needs the most work. There is also real value in choosing the right people to ask in the first place. Honest feedback tends to be most useful when it comes from someone who genuinely understands the situation, and who is actually willing to be straightforward with you rather than simply agreeable.Bill Gates' quote is ultimately about something genuinely ordinary, simply allowing other people to show us what we honestly cannot see for ourselves. Real improvement is rarely a single dramatic moment. Far more often, it comes through a series of small corrections made gradually over time, a better explanation offered here, a slightly different approach tried there, a habit finally changed after someone else genuinely pointed it out. The person offering the feedback may only be sharing a few honest sentences. For the person genuinely willing to actually listen, those few sentences can sometimes reveal an entirely different way of looking at the work, the situation, or even themselves.
Article Summary: Bill Gates: "We all need people who will give us feedback. That's how we improve" The Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist made the point in a TED talk. The real story behind this quote is that people need honest feedback from others.

Article Title: Apple shares owner since its IPO days, Florida billionaire buys Ferrari’s first EV, designed by iPhone designer Jony Ive; 87-year-old is 'known for' never selling ...
Article Text:
Long-time Apple share owner Ferrari Luce bought for $40 million

From owning Apple shares to a Jony Ive-designed Ferrari

Ferrari Luce is the company's first electric production car

Florida billionaire and longtime Apple investor Herbert A. Wertheim has paid $40 million for the first production Ferrari Luce, the automaker’s first fully electric production car. The 87-year-old investor bought Apple shares when the company went public in 1980 and is known for holding onto his investments for decades. The Ferrari Luce he bought, has been designed in collaboration with LoveFrom, the creative studio founded by former Apple design chief Jony Ive and designer Marc Newson. The car, known as Chassis 0, was sold at an RM Sotheby’s auction in Monterey for more than 36 times its $1.1 million presale estimate.Herbert A. Wertheim bought the first production Ferrari Luce at the RM Sotheby’s Monterey auction. The entire $40 million hammer price will go to the Ferrari Foundation. The car is marked as Chassis 0, giving it a special place in the Luce’s production history. Ferrari’s Tailor Made division also created a unique specification for the vehicle.The car has a one-off Madreperla Semi-Gloss finish that can shift between green and violet depending on the lighting and viewing angle.The interior uses Perla Le Mans metallic leather with Grigio Corvara details.Herbert A. Wertheim's connection with Apple goes back to the company's 1980 IPO. He bought shares when Apple went public and continued building his position over the years. Forbes reported in 2019 that Wertheim owned 1.25 million Apple shares, which were then worth about $195 million. His portfolio has also included companies such as Microsoft, Google, GE, BP and Bank of America.The Ferrari purchase has a connection to Apple's design history because the Luce was created in collaboration with LoveFrom, the design studio founded by Jony Ive after his long career at Apple. Ive played a key role in the design of several major Apple products, including the iPhone and Apple Watch.The Luce is Ferrari's first fully electric production automobile. The car uses four electric motors that together produce 1,036 horsepower. Ferrari claims the Luce can accelerate from 0 to 62 mph in 2.5 seconds, while its top speed is around 193 mph. The car uses a 122-kWh battery and has a claimed range of about 329 miles under the WLTP standard. It can support charging at up to 350kW.
Article Summary: Florida billionaire and longtime Apple investor Herbert A. Wertheim has paid $40 million for the first production Ferrari Luce. The 87-year-old investor bought Apple shares when the company went public in 1980 and is known for holding onto his investments for decades. Ferrari's first fully electric production car, the Luce has been designed in collaboration with LoveFrom, the creative studio founded by former Apple design chief Jony Ive.

Article Title: Chinese AI lab Z.ai that Sam Altman and Dario Amodei complained about has a warning similar to biggest American AI companies
Article Text:
What Z.ai announced

How it stacks up against US models

Z.ai's defenders-first framing

The catch

China‑based AI lab Z.ai has warned that its latest model, GLM‑5.3, is so capable at finding and exploiting security flaws that the company will delay public release of the model weights for two weeks, according to a report by Axios. The lab said it is testing and strengthening safety and security controls before wider availability. The warning from Z.ai echoes concerns raised by Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, who have previously cautioned about the risks posed by powerful open‑weight models. Both executives have argued that models capable of cyber exploitation could be misused if released without strong safeguards, highlighting the growing tension between innovation and security in AI development.AI models capable of identifying and exploiting cyber vulnerabilities carry major implications for both sides of the security equation, offering real gains for defenders trying to patch systems, but also for hackers looking to scale up attacks.Recenlty, Z.ai warned that its newest model, GLM-5.3, has become so capable at finding and exploiting security flaws that the company is delaying the public release of the model's weights by two weeks while it tests and strengthens its safety and security controls.The company specifically trained GLM-5.3 to improve at vulnerability discovery by letting it practice cyber tasks in controlled environments, and is rolling out a tiered access program that, for now, limits access to GLM-5.3 to selected security partners operating in controlled settings.On CyberGym, a benchmark that measures how well models can find known security vulnerabilities, GLM-5.3 scored 84.5%, outperforming both Anthropic's Fable 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol. On ExploitBench, which evaluates a model's ability to reason through and construct exploits for real vulnerabilities, GLM-5.3 trailed only Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol among the models Z.ai tested it against.According to a new disclosure site the company released recently, Z.ai says its GLM models have already identified more than 2,400 security flaws, including over 1,000 rated as critical or high severity, with some of those vulnerabilities found in the Linux kernel and in widely used VMware and Apache projects. The company is framing GLM-5.3's release primarily as a benefit to defenders rather than a risk, writing on X that an open world cannot have only open attack surfaces, arguing that it must also have an open shield. Alongside the model announcement, Z.ai also introduced a new program letting open-source maintainers have a GLM model scan their repositories for bugs.Z.ai's models have already shown some practical value on the defensive side: Hugging Face has said it used GLM-5.2 to investigate a recent breach involving OpenAI's models, after guardrails built into U.S. frontier models declined to assist with that investigation.Z.ai acknowledged in its X post that once GLM-5.3's weights become public, the company will have no way to control how people modify or use the model going forward, a limitation inherent to open-weight releases more broadly. Meanwhile, the Trump administration appears to be weighing potential approaches to regulating open-source AI models as their capabilities increasingly rival those of their closed, proprietary counterparts.
Article Summary: Z.ai's GLM-5.3 is so capable at finding and exploiting security flaws that the company will delay public release of the model weights for two weeks. The lab said it is testing and strengthening safety and security controls before wider availability.

Article Title: Secret tracking device placed in rare book ends up in Amazon processing facility, destroying books to train AI models is 'all' the Vegas warehouse does
Article Text:
An AirTag hidden in a rare book led to Amazon's Las Vegas warehouse, where books are cut apart and scanned for AI training.

AirTag trail ended at the Amazon's LAS8 warehouse in North Las Vegas

Why AI training data companies want books printed before 2022

Rare booksellers in the UK and Ireland are refusing bulk AI orders

A bookseller who suspected that an anonymous order for around 1,000 titles was headed into an AI training pipeline decided to stop guessing. Working with 404 Media, the seller slipped an Apple AirTag into one volume and shipped the order through Biblio, a marketplace that keeps buyers anonymous. The tracker flew out of a California airport, landed outside Milwaukee, then sat for two weeks in a distribution warehouse near Kenosha Regional Airport before heading west by truck, pausing overnight at a travel centre near Grand Junction, Colorado.Its final stop was an Amazon warehouse called LAS8 in Las Vegas. More precisely, the north end of it, which houses a separate Amazon operation coded VGT3, where books arrive, lose their bindings to a cutter, get scanned, and are thrown out. 404Media found VGT3 staff describing the work on an Amazon employee forum, one of them writing that "all we do is scan books." The site's symbol, painted at the entrance, is a Tyrannosaurus rex holding an open book.Amazon has not disputed any of it. A spokesperson said the company buys books through commercial channels to help develop and improve the products and services its customers use, and declined to answer why the books are cut, how many such facilities it runs worldwide, or how it views the backlash.LAS8 otherwise operates as a print-on-demand site, which is what made the destination confusing at first. The detail that matters more is what workers say they scan first: the barcode. Booksellers have long suspected AI firms are working methodically through the global ISBN list, and one seller noted that the huge orders never included the truly rare titles that predate ISBNs entirely.The pattern is not new either. Inc. found Amazon Seller Forum posts from September 2024 describing bursts of orders bound for the same location, one seller reporting 68 orders from a single buyer, another describing 48 orders landing around 4am, all University Press titles. Sellers thought it was a scam. An Amazon representative told them the orders were valid.Amazon builds its own Nova family of large language models and pitches them as frontier-class. Models like that need enormous volumes of human-written text, and the open internet has already been scraped clean. Print books hold text that never went online, arranged neatly, and anything printed before 2022 comes with a guarantee no webpage can offer: no chatbot wrote it. Train on too much synthetic text and quality degrades in a loop researchers call model collapse.That explains the orders sellers keep flagging worldwide since roughly May. Large, randomly assorted, and placed by buyers who never haggle. Tomás Kenny of Kennys Bookshop in Galway said AI is "terrifying our industry" and plans to refuse orders he believes are bound for training data.The practice surfaced through the authors' lawsuit against Anthropic, which exposed Project Panama and ended in an approved $1.5 billion settlement. The judge treated the destruction of the original copy as a point in Anthropic's favour on fair use. Anthropic says none of its acquisition programmes buy and destroy rare or antiquarian books.The bookseller who planted the AirTag told 404 Media that books carry historical, intellectual and sentimental value alongside the sticker price. None of that survives the trip to Las Vegas. The buyers want the words, and the spine is the part that gets in the way.
Article Summary: Rare bookseller slips AirTag into one volume and sends it through Biblio. AirTag leads to Amazon's LAS8 warehouse in North Las Vegas, where books are cut apart and scanned for AI training. Amazon has not disputed any of it and declined to answer why the books were cut.

Article Title: In 1989, Apple buried about 2,700 unsold Lisa computers in a Utah landfill after its $10,000 machine failed; 37 years later, it remains one of the strangest product failures in the company's history
Article Text:
Steve Jobs poses with Lisa computer (Getty images)

A Lisa, dumped and destroyed (Picture: Hackaday)

Attempt to save Lisa failed

Brochure showing Lisa 1 screen and Twiggy floppy drives (Picture source: Medium.com)

Lisa failed, but changed computing

Before the Macintosh became one of Apple's defining products, the company had another computer that failed in the market. In September 1989, Apple took an unusual step with thousands of unsold Lisa computers. About 2,700 machines were buried at a landfill in Logan, Utah, bringing an end to the story of one of the company's most ambitious but unsuccessful computers.The Lisa had been launched in 1983 as Apple's first attempt at a modern computer built around a graphical interface. According to The Verge, it had a mouse, windows, icons and menus, features that later became standard on desktop computers. The Lisa had them a year before the Macintosh was released.But the computer struggled in the market. It carried a price tag of about $10,000 and had hardware problems. It was also overshadowed by the cheaper Macintosh that Apple was preparing to introduce. Even after being discounted, upgraded and renamed the Macintosh XL, the Lisa lasted only about two years before Apple dropped it in 1985. After being discontinued, thousands of Lisa machines were still left over.A computer salesman named Bob Cook saw an opportunity in the unwanted stock.He had been selling older computers at discounted prices and had previously taken about 3,500 Apple III computers from Apple in 1985. A year later, he took on the last 7,000 Lisas.Cook was an Apple reseller who believed older computers could still find buyers. “Computers were supposed to be leading edge, so nobody was thinking about selling the trailing edge of high technology,” Cook told The Verge.Rather than simply selling Lisa, Cook worked on improving the machines so they could compete with newer Mac models. He estimated that he spent $200,000 on research and development, upgrading the hardware and operating system.Cook gave the upgraded computer a new name. “It was something different. So we called it the ‘Lisa Professional,’” he said. But the effort eventually came to an end, and the remaining Lisas faced a very different fate.Soonafter, Apple buried about 2,700 unsold Lisa computers at the Logan landfill in September 1989. Landfill workers drove bulldozers over the computers before they were buried.The Lisa's failure was closely linked to its price and its timing. At around $10,000, it was far too expensive for many potential buyers. Its hardware problems also worked against it, while the Macintosh offered a cheaper alternative.Yet the Lisa had introduced ideas that would become central to personal computing. Veteran technology journalist Steven Levy described its ease of use in an interview with The Verge.“The Lisa was the first computer out there that you didn’t have to struggle with a big computer manual or even hire a consultant to use,” Levy said. “You could understand it out of the box and start using it.”The Lisa therefore occupied an unusual place in Apple's history. It failed to become a successful mass-market product, but its graphical approach helped shape the kind of computers consumers would later expect.The Computer History Museum says Lisa had 1MB RAM, a 12-inch black-and-white display, two 5.25-inch floppy drives and a 5MB hard drive. An archived 1983 technical article says the project representedmore than 200 person-years of work and $50 million in development.Lisa project started in 1978, several years before its launch. Steve Jobs initially led the project but was removed from it in 1982. After that, he moved his attention to the Macintosh project.
Article Summary: Apple buried about 2,700 unsold Lisa computers at a landfill in Utah in 1989. The Lisa had been launched in 1983 as Apple's first attempt at a modern computer built around a graphical interface. It had a mouse, windows, icons and menus, features that later became standard on desktop computers.

Article Title: How Silverfox cybercriminal group is using Claude to target companies in India and other Asian countries
Article Text:
Representative Image

“SilverFox is one of the most active threat groups in the whole APAC region. They get into targets through three simple routes: fake websites, phishing emails, and harmful files spread via social messaging apps. They inject malware used for long-term cyberespionage and sensitive data gathering. Our recent analysis showed they are now distributing fake Claude for Windows, macOS, and Linux, leveraging AI use in companies to crack into their targets’ security defenses,”

How SilverFox uses fake Claude apps to target companies

“list of tax violations.”

SilverFox attacks remain concentrated in Asia

AI is changing the speed and scale of cyberattacks

“In this particular case, disclosed by our Sysdig, the malicious AI agent completed the entire cycle of diagnosing a failed attempt, correcting its approach, and launching a new attack in just 31 seconds, far outpacing the response capabilities of most human defenders. Beyond speed, JADEPUFFER also demonstrates an unprecedented level of autonomy. It shows that AI agents are now capable of making independent decisions throughout the attack process, effectively replicating the reasoning of an experienced human attacker without direct oversight,”

How companies can defend against AI-powered attacks

SilverFox, an Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) group, is using fake Claude apps to target companies in India and other countries in the Asia Pacific region. According to researchers from Kaspersky’s Global Research and Analysis Team (GReAT), the cybercriminal group is exploiting the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in businesses to distribute malware and gain access to target networks.explains Ye Jin (Seth), Lead Security Researcher at Kaspersky GReAT.Kaspersky researchers said SilverFox has used a multi-stage attack process and segmented infrastructure, with different addresses and domains used at different stages. The approach can make it harder for security teams to identify and block the complete attack chain.The group’s recent campaign targeted organisations in India, Indonesia, South Africa and Russia across industrial, consulting, trade and transportation sectors. Attackers sent phishing emails designed to appear like official tax audit notifications or messages asking recipients to download an archive containing a supposedMore than 1,600 malicious emails were detected in January-February 2026, according to Kaspersky data. The emails often used a sense of authority and urgency, similar to messages about taxes, to trick people into opening malicious files and launching the attacks.More recent findings indicate that SilverFox has expanded its tactics to fake versions of Claude for Windows, macOS and Linux. Claude is an AI assistant developed by Anthropic that can be used for writing, coding, analysing documents and other tasks.Kaspersky said the APAC region accounts for the largest share of SilverFox’s malicious activity, with attack volumes exceeding those recorded across other regions combined.“Based on our current threat data, Greater China is SilverFox’s main target, with over 90% of all its attacks targeting the region. Mainland China alone makes up 71%. Myanmar, Cambodia and Singapore also see lots of attacks. These are the next hotspots we need to watch,” adds Ye Jin.Manufacturing accounts for more than one-third of the group’s attacks, making it the most targeted industry in Kaspersky’s current data. IT and services are also frequently targeted, while healthcare and finance remain among the sectors facing attacks from the group.Kaspersky’s Ye Jin also highlighted the emergence of AI-driven attacks that can automate decisions and parts of the attack process. One example is JADEPUFFER, described as an LLM-driven ransomware attack that demonstrated how an AI agent could analyse a failed attempt, change its approach and launch another attack.he explains.Another example highlighted by the researcher is ChatGPhish, an indirect prompt injection technique in which malicious instructions are hidden inside webpages. When a user asks an AI assistant to summarise such a page, the embedded instructions can potentially be processed by the AI and surfaced as part of its response.Kaspersky also pointed to VoidLink, an AI-assisted cloud-native malware framework reported in January 2026, as an example of how generative AI can reduce the technical effort required to develop malware.Kaspersky recommends that organisations adapt their security measures as attackers increasingly use AI and automated techniques. Its suggested measures include proactive AI-driven threat hunting to identify unknown threats, alongside Zero Trust architecture that verifies access requests rather than automatically trusting users or devices inside a network.The company also recommends a systematic defence covering endpoints, networks, applications and data. Another approach is using AI models and other dual-use AI technologies to improve threat detection and response and adapt security measures as attack techniques change.The growing use of AI by both attackers and defenders means organisations need to account for AI-assisted phishing, malware distribution and automated attack processes alongside conventional cybersecurity threats.
Article Summary: SilverFox, an Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) group, is using fake Claude apps to target companies in India and other countries in the Asia Pacific region. The group’s recent campaign targeted organisations in India, Indonesia, South Africa and Russia across industrial, consulting, trade and transportation sectors.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Andrew Carnegie: People who are unable to motivate themselves must be content with mediocrity
Article Text:
What Andrew Carnegie's quote implies

Andrew Carnegie's life and self-motivation

Legendary American industrialist Andrew Carnegie is known for several quotes on self-motivation. Some of them continue to be referenced in discussions on personal and professional growth even today, particularly in contexts involving career development, leadership and goal-setting. One of his quotes reads: "People who are unable to motivate themselves must be content with mediocrity, no matter how impressive their other talents."The statement has been quoted in a variety of contexts, from workplace training materials to motivational writing to public speeches, to distinguish between having ability and actually doing something with that ability. The quote does not specify a profession or context, which makes it applicable in many settings, from business and sports to education and the arts. This means talent alone will not yield results, and self-motivation is another prerequisite.Carnegie’s quote suggests that motivation is an element of its own, distinct from skill and knowledge. This quote implies that someone might have great skills in a certain area, but if they don’t have the motivation to use those skills regularly, those skills might not produce great results. The quote describes self-motivation as something that must come from within and not depend on outside circumstances or acknowledgement.Andrew Carnegie was a Scottish-American industrialist who made his career in the steel industry in the late 19th century. Carnegie was born in Dunfermline, Scotland, in 1835, and immigrated with his family to the United States in 1848, working as a boy in a factory before moving through jobs in telegraphy and railroads. He later founded the Carnegie Steel Company, which was sold in 1901 to become part of US Steel.Often, his rise from factory worker to one of the world’s largest steel operations is mentioned alongside his thoughts on ambition, persistence, and self-driven effort. In the latter part of his life, Carnegie devoted much of his wealth to philanthropy, funding libraries, educational institutions and research organisations throughout the United States and other countries.
Article Summary: Andrew Carnegie was a Scottish-American industrialist who made his career in the steel industry in the late 19th century. One of his quotes reads: "People who are unable to motivate themselves must be content with mediocrity, no matter how impressive their other talents" The statement has been quoted in a variety of contexts, from workplace training materials to motivational writing to public speeches.

And that AI can’t really do,” Wilson said, as per a report by The Wall Street Journal. He pointed out that quantum systems will unlock solutions to complex challenges that conventional computers take too long to resolve and that standard AI cannot properly handle. While exact rollout timelines and the precise scale of early competitive benefits remain uncertain, Wilson expressed firm conviction that early adopters will reap significant rewards.Within Allstate, an internal quantum unit of 10 specialists is actively expanding. The team is researching practical applications, such as analysing intricate risk variables and interdependencies to generate sharper, more accurate pricing structures that reflect true policy risk levels.Wilson summarised his advice to corporate leadership in four words: “Get on the train”. Drawing parallels to the sudden surge of generative AI, Wilson cautioned that organisations delaying their quantum strategy will struggle to benefit once the tech matures.According to Wilson, the objective is building foundational organisational knowledge. Companies must engage with quantum advancements early so their underlying technology infrastructure is ready to plug into quantum systems when the time comes.“You can invest in quantum, but really the thing is, do you know enough about quantum? And are you engaged enough in the development of quantum so that you know how to build your current system so that it’s ready when quantum is ready?” he said.

Article Title: A high school student won America’s top science award for solving a centuries-old Geometry problem; how his work on 146 rare shapes can change the future of medicine
Article Text:
Image credit: Society for Science

Connor Hill’s geometry research identifies 146 rare shapes

How Connor Hill’s math connects to medicine and science

Why mathematical proofs matter to medical research

Connor Hill’s next step after Regeneron Science Talent Search

“Math is the language that makes scientific ideas usable.”

US high school student Connor Hill won first place at the 2026 Regeneron Science Talent Search (STS). He has won the award for solving a longstanding problem in geometry involving a class of shapes known as noble polyhedra. His research produced a complete classification of these geometric objects, identifying two infinite families and 146 isolated examples, and earned him the top award from the Society for Science’s competition.The work is rooted in a centuries-old mathematical tradition dating back to Plato and the early study of geometry, but its significance extends beyond the shapes themselves. Hill’s approach involved translating a potentially infinite geometric problem into a finite one using algebra and polynomials. That method of reducing a complex set of possibilities to a manageable number is also used in modern scientific research, including biology, protein structure and drug discovery.Hill’s research focused on noble polyhedra, geometric objects defined by symmetry in which all faces are identical, and all vertices are identical. A cube is a basic example of a highly symmetrical polyhedron, while noble polyhedra relax some of the restrictions found in classical shapes such as the Platonic solids.Hill said his interest in the subject began through an online mathematics community where he encountered the open question surrounding noble polyhedra. What initially appeared to be a search for additional examples eventually developed into a complete proof and classification.A central part of the research was finding a way to reduce the number of possibilities. Rather than attempting to examine an unlimited number of geometric arrangements directly, Hill connected the problem to algebra, including polynomials, which allowed him to convert it into a finite problem that could be solved.The result was the identification of two infinite families of noble polyhedra along with 146 isolated examples.The connection between Hill’s geometry research and medicine lies in the mathematical method rather than in the geometric shapes themselves. Modern biology often involves systems with a large number of possible configurations, making it necessary to identify which possibilities are stable, relevant or biologically meaningful.Henry Wei, MD, Executive Director, Development Innovation at Regeneron, discussed this connection with Hill. Wei is a physician-scientist working at the intersection of biology and medicine.One example is protein structure. Proteins can take on many possible configurations, but only some are stable or relevant to biological processes. Mathematics can help researchers narrow those possibilities and identify structures that may matter for understanding disease or developing medicines.The same principle applies to drug discovery, where researchers need to work through complex biological systems and determine which interactions or structures are most relevant.Hill’s work also demonstrates how a problem can be transformed by moving between different areas of mathematics. His research connected discrete geometry with algebraic geometry to establish a finite framework for a problem that initially involved an effectively unlimited set of possibilities.Modern scientific research frequently uses models and approximations to understand complex systems. Mathematical methods can provide another approach by establishing exact relationships and reducing large sets of possibilities to smaller, more defined problems.Hill said the method used in his project could apply beyond noble polyhedra because the same approach can be useful wherever researchers encounter structure, symmetry or a large number of possibilities that need to be narrowed down.Wei similarly pointed to the role of mathematics in making complex biological systems more understandable. Problems involving protein folding, disease progression, and interactions between treatments and the human body all require researchers to identify patterns within large, complex systems.The connection does not mean Hill’s 146 geometric examples directly produce new medicines. Instead, his research illustrates how mathematical techniques for simplifying complex problems can also be relevant to scientific fields where researchers face similarly large sets of possibilities.Hill is set to attend MIT this fall, with his education supported in part by his winnings from the 2026 Regeneron Science Talent Search.His research also reflects the role of curiosity-driven mathematics in scientific work. Hill said his project did not begin with a planned breakthrough. It developed gradually as he explored an open mathematical question and connected different areas of mathematics to solve it.The broader relevance of the work lies in that process: reducing a problem that appears infinite to a finite set, establishing an exact solution and then applying the underlying method to other fields where complexity needs to be reduced.As Hill puts it,Science provides concepts, while mathematics formalises them and makes them applicable to specific problems.Beyond university, Hill intends to publish his results and develop educational resources to help students explore advanced geometry, while also collaborating with researchers to adapt his algebraic approach for computational problems in other scientific disciplines.
Article Summary: US high school student Connor Hill won first place at the 2026 Regeneron Science Talent Search. He has won the award for solving a longstanding problem in geometry involving a class of shapes known as noble polyhedra. His research produced a complete classification of these geometric objects, identifying two infinite families and 146 isolated examples.

Article Title: Tech CEO who sacked employees in a 79-second Zoom call has been fired; tells company board: I want my job back, willing to work for ...
Article Text:

Vishal Garg asks Better Home & Finance board to reinstate him

Better board replaced Vishal Garg with Daniel Lewis

"(Lewis') thoughts about cost savings were good. His ideas about innovation were not,"

"It's so much easier when we're this close for someone to come in and say that they could have done better."

"The board made a mistake."

Better Home & Finance fired its CEO Vishal Garg earlier this month. This ended his latest tenure at the mortgage technology company after several years of financial losses. This included a failed refinancing business and efforts to rebuild the company around artificial intelligence (AI). Garg, who became widely known after laying off about 900 employees during a 79-second Zoom call in 2021, is now asking the company's board to reinstate him as CEO, offering to work for $1 a year until Better returns to profitability, after which he says he would step down.Garg said.Garg remains a member of Better's board and says he has voting support through his Class B shares, which carry special voting powers, along with shares held by a group of early investors. He has retained lawyer Alex Spiro, a partner at Quinn Emanuel, and recently sent a letter to the board requesting reinstatement, asking it to reverse its August 3 decision.Garg said.Garg acknowledged that the 2021 Zoom layoffs damaged his reputation and said the incident remains associated with his tenure at Better. He described himself as "hard-nosed" while arguing that Lewis had convinced the board he had not pushed the company and its employees hard enough.Daniel Lewis, a hedge fund manager, joined Better's board on July 27 and replaced Garg as CEO a week later. Garg said Lewis approached him about six months earlier with suggestions to reduce costs and improve profitability.Garg argued.Garg also accused Lewis of concealing his intentions while advising him and seeking a position on the board. "I suspect he always wanted to become CEO," said Garg.Lewis posted on X on August 4, "There was never a $BETR without @vishal_better. That demands respect."Better and Lewis did not respond to a request for comment.The company's stock has fallen 45% since Lewis became CEO, according to the report. Garg said some investors contacted him after his removal and urged him to return to the CEO role.His tenure has also included a leave of absence following the 2021 layoffs, a whistleblower lawsuit that was later dropped, a Securities and Exchange Commission investigation that did not result in action, and a 2023 SPAC merger after which the company's stock fell sharply.Garg also claimed that he was removed just as Better was approaching a potential turnaround after its refinancing business declined sharply following the pandemic-era mortgage boom. He said the company's annual sales fell from $1.5 billion in 2021 to $70 million in 2023, and are now on track for about $200 million this year.
Article Summary: Vishal Garg is asking the Better Home & Finance board to reinstate him as CEO. Garg became widely known after laying off about 900 employees during a 79-second Zoom call in 2021. Daniel Lewis, a hedge fund manager, replaced Garg as CEO a week later.

Article Title: USB4 vs USB-C explained: Speeds, cable lengths and the one spec that nobody reads
Article Text:
USB-C is the plug. USB4 is the standard. Knowing which is which decides what you should pay.

The difference between USB4 and USB-C is simple: USB4 is a shape, the USB-C is a set of rules

Is USB-C the same as USB4? Every USB4 cable is USB-C, but almost no USB-C cable is USB4

How to tell if your laptop has USB4, because the port almost never says so

USB4 vs Thunderbolt 4 comes down to certification, not speed, since both stop at 40Gbps

USB4 cable length is the spec nobody reads and the one that quietly ruins setups

USB4 vs USB-C : Which one to buy, and which one do you really need

There is a drawer in most homes now that holds eight or nine cables with the same oval plug on the end, and no way of telling which one is which. One of them charges a laptop. One transfers at speeds that feel like punishment. One came free with a pair of earbuds and does almost nothing beyond keeping them alive. They are physically identical, they all fit every port in the house, and the only difference between them is invisible.That is the whole USB4 versus USB-C problem in one image. USB-C is the shape. USB4 is what the wires inside are allowed to do. The two words turn up on the same spec sheet constantly, often in the same line, which is why they get treated as versions of each other. They are not. A laptop advertising "USB-C ports" has told you nothing about speed, video output or charging. A laptop advertising USB4 has committed to something specific.USB-C arrived in 2014 as a physical redesign. Twenty-four pins, reversible, small enough for a phone and sturdy enough for a workstation. It solved the flipping problem and nothing else. Speed, video and power delivery were all left to whatever protocol the manufacturer decided to run over those pins, which could be anything from USB 2.0 at 480Mbps upward.USB4 is that protocol. The USB Implementers Forum published it in 2019, built on a Thunderbolt 3 specification Intel donated to the group. The number people quote is 40Gbps, but the more useful change is tunnelling. USB4 carries DisplayPort and PCIe traffic alongside ordinary data, and reallocates bandwidth on the fly depending on whether you are copying a file or pushing pixels to a monitor. That is what makes single-cable docking work at all. One connection to a dock and the laptop picks up displays, storage, ethernet and up to 100W of charging, with the Extended Power Range spec reaching 240W on hardware that supports it.Worth sitting with, because it explains most of the confusion. The relationship runs one way. USB4 requires the USB-C connector, so every USB4 cable ends in one. USB-C requires nothing in return, so the majority of USB-C cables in circulation are running much older standards underneath.The chain runs at the speed of its slowest link, and there are three links. Plug a 40Gbps SSD into a USB 3.2 Gen 2 port and you get 10Gbps. Plug that same SSD into a proper USB4 port using a cable that came free in a phone box, and you may get 480Mbps, because the cable is the bottleneck and nothing on screen will tell you so. Files will still copy. They will just take an amount of time that makes no sense given what you paid for the drive.Naming has not helped. USB 3.0 became USB 3.1 Gen 1, then USB 3.2 Gen 1, three names for identical 5Gbps hardware. The USB-IF's response has been to abandon generation numbers in consumer-facing marketing and push speed logos instead, so packaging now reads "USB 40Gbps" or "USB 80Gbps." That is a real improvement, though it only applies to products certified after the change.On the hardware itself, look for a small USB4 marking beside the port, or a Thunderbolt lightning bolt, since Thunderbolt 4 and 5 ports also carry USB4. Plenty of laptops print nothing at all, in which case the spec sheet is the only honest source. Manufacturers also mix port types on the same machine, so the two ports on the left may run at 40Gbps while the one on the right handles 10Gbps and no video. Checking each port individually is tedious and occasionally necessary.The two are close enough that the distinction is mostly about guarantees. Thunderbolt 4 sets a floor: two 4K displays or one 8K, 32Gbps of PCIe bandwidth for storage, mandatory charging support on at least one port. USB4 makes several of those optional, which means one USB4 laptop can drive dual monitors and an external GPU while another handles a single display and refuses the eGPU entirely. Both are correctly labelled.Above that sits USB4 Version 2.0, ratified in 2022 and now on flagship laptops, which doubles throughput to 80Gbps and can run asymmetrically at 120Gbps in one direction for high-refresh displays. Thunderbolt 5 matches it with stricter certification. Whether any of this registers depends entirely on what you connect. For someone editing 4K footage off an external drive, 40Gbps against 10Gbps is the difference between a short wait and a coffee break. For a wired mouse, a keyboard and a printer, it is theoretical.Passive USB4 cables hold full speed only over short runs, roughly 0.8 metres per the specification, which is why certified ones are conspicuously stubby. Longer passive cables drop to half rate. Active cables carry signal-conditioning chips that maintain throughput over greater distances, but they cost more and are less reliably backward compatible with ordinary USB-C peripherals.Power ratings vary independently of all this. A cable can pass 40Gbps and still refuse to charge a laptop, because the wattage it supports is a separate line on a spec sheet most listings never bother to include. In India, a certified 40Gbps cable from a known brand generally runs between Rs 1,500 and Rs 4,000 against a few hundred rupees for an unmarked one. The cheap cable is not fake so much as unspecified, and unspecified is the problem. If a listing states neither a data rate nor a wattage, assume the worst of both.There is no choosing between them, which is the first thing to settle. Buy a USB4 cable and you get USB-C by definition. The actual decision is whether the USB4 premium buys you anything.If you run a dock, an external SSD, an eGPU or a second monitor off your laptop, it does, and the appeal of USB4 is that you stop having to think about any of this. Compliant devices at both ends will negotiate the fastest speeds they support without intervention, and the cable still charges older USB-C hardware because backward compatibility is built in.If all you do is charge a phone and plug in a mouse, it does not. A dedicated 100W power delivery cable running USB 2.0 sells for Rs 400 to Rs 900 and will charge exactly as fast as the Rs 4,000 one, because charging wattage and data throughput are separate specifications that happen to share a plug. Most people need one good USB4 cable for the desk and cheap PD cables everywhere else. Buying the expensive one four times over is the common mistake, and it costs more than the cable that actually needed replacing.Which brings it back to the drawer. It was never lying. It simply never said anything, and neither did most of the people selling the contents. Sort it once, put tape on the fast ones, and the question stops coming up.
Article Summary: The difference between USB4 and USB-C is simple: USB4 is a shape, the USB- C is a set of rules. Knowing which is which decides what you should pay.USB4 vs Thunderbolt 4 comes down to certification, not speed, since both stop at 40Gbps. USB4 carries DisplayPort and PCIe traffic alongside ordinary data.

iOS 27 beta 5 reportedly lists six unreleased iPhones

What Tesla’s biggest investor Ross Gerber said

Apple iPhone 18 could face higher costs

Apple’s pricing strategy

Ross Gerber, co-founder, president and CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management and one of Tesla's most prominent individual investors is now telling consumers that if they are in the market for a new iPhone, then they may want to move before Apple ’s next-generation lineup arrives.
